name: Prompterjack
tagline: Design multi-agent AI systems visually, export runnable code for five frameworks.
description: Full-stack prompt-engineering and agent-design platform: pick an architecture style, design multi-agent systems visually, export production-ready code for Strands, OpenAI Agents, LangChain/LangGraph and LlamaIndex. Codebase-aware prompt generation, maintainability scoring, marketplace, real-time co-editing.
architecture: Turborepo monorepo. React SPA on the edge, Hono API on Cloudflare Workers, Neon Postgres for state, Stripe for billing. The canvas is the source of truth: a crew graph compiles down to whichever framework you export to.
highlights: Visual canvas for supervisor/worker, router, and pipeline crew shapes
One graph exports to five agent frameworks — Strands, OpenAI Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex
Prompt linter scores maintainability and flags ambiguity before you ship
Codebase-aware generation: point it at a repo, get prompts that know your types
Real-time co-editing and a marketplace for published crews
lessons: Agent frameworks disagree about everything except the shape of the graph. Model the graph, generate the framework.

name: Claude Work Manager
tagline: Run a fleet of Claude Code agents across git worktrees — from your phone.
description: Self-hosted, mobile-first dashboard for concurrent Claude Code sessions: spawn an isolated git worktree per agent, chat with each one, watch localhost previews of their dev servers, and commit/push from the couch. Rides the claude CLI you're already logged into — no API keys stored anywhere.
architecture: A Node server wraps the local `claude` CLI. One git worktree per agent means agents never fight over the working tree. The browser talks to the server; the server talks to the CLI you already authenticated.
highlights: One isolated git worktree per agent — parallel work with no merge chaos
Mobile-first: review, steer, and push from a phone
Live localhost previews of each agent's dev server
No API keys stored: it borrows the CLI session you already have
Commit and push per worktree without leaving the dashboard
lessons: Isolation is the whole trick. Once each agent owns a worktree, running five at once stops being scary.

name: Worktree Optimiser
tagline: Every branch of a repo as its own containerised dev server, routed by hostname.
description: Run all your worktrees at once — main.localhost, fix-login.localhost — each in its own Docker container behind Traefik, managed from one dashboard. Review a PR and your own work side by side in two tabs. Ships an MCP server so coding agents can drive it too.
architecture: Traefik does hostname routing; every worktree gets a container and a `<branch>.localhost` name. A dashboard drives the lifecycle, and an MCP server exposes the same lifecycle to coding agents as tools.
highlights: `main.localhost`, `fix-login.localhost` — every branch live at once
Container per worktree, routed by Traefik, no port juggling
Review a PR and your own branch side by side in two tabs
MCP server so Claude Code can spin environments up and down itself
MIT licensed
lessons: Anything a human clicks in a dashboard, an agent should be able to call as a tool. Building the MCP layer second was a mistake worth not repeating.

name: ALFRED
tagline: Local-first multi-agent life-optimization system. Your hardware, your data, no cloud.
description: Decomposes goals into weekly plans a Conductor reconciles against real capacity, delivers over Discord/Telegram, watches what happens, and adapts. Every tool call passes an allowlist, capability tier and audit trail. 529 offline tests in CI.
architecture: Local models via Ollama, SQLite for state, Pydantic contracts between every agent. A Conductor reconciles specialist plans against real capacity before anything reaches you. Chat surfaces are Discord and Telegram.
highlights: Runs entirely on your hardware — no cloud, no data leaving the house
Conductor reconciles specialist plans against actual weekly capacity
Every tool call checked against an allowlist and a capability tier, then audited
Adapts from what actually happened, not what was planned
529 offline tests in CI — the whole suite runs with no network
MIT licensed
lessons: A planner that ignores capacity is a to-do list generator. The Conductor exists because the first version cheerfully planned 60-hour weeks.

name: QuantFlex
tagline: Free web derivatives pricing engine with hand-rolled Monte Carlo, PDE and autodiff.
description: Prices vanillas, American options, exotics and baskets under GBM, Merton and Heston with hand-rolled solvers and Greeks from a custom autodiff tape. Every price validated against analytic anchors; every Greek triple-verified against JAX.
architecture: Hand-rolled numerics in NumPy — Monte Carlo, finite-difference PDE, and a custom reverse-mode autodiff tape for Greeks. FastAPI in front, Vue 3 SPA on top, Cloud Run underneath. JAX is used only as an oracle in tests.
highlights: Vanillas, Americans, exotics and baskets under GBM, Merton jump-diffusion and Heston
Greeks from a custom autodiff tape, not bumped finite differences
Every price anchored to a closed-form or published benchmark
Every Greek triple-verified: tape vs bump vs JAX
Separate landing site with live engine output and a daily market feed
lessons: Write the oracle before the solver. The analytic anchors caught more bugs than the unit tests did.

name: QuantLens
tagline: AI-narrated portfolio dashboard — Sharpe, VaR, Monte Carlo, factors, RAG Q&A.
description: Quant-finance Spring Boot backend plus Vue 3 SPA: P&L, risk metrics, Fama-French factors and cointegration pairs, narrated by Spring AI with RAG over pgvector. One docker compose up, no API keys, three seeded demo personas.
architecture: Spring Boot 3.5 runs the quant engine; Spring AI runs tool-calling and RAG over pgvector, with an embedded MCP server. Vue 3 on the front. `docker compose up` brings the whole thing, seed data included.
highlights: P&L, Sharpe, VaR, Monte Carlo, Fama-French factors, cointegration pairs
The AI narrates real engine output — it calls tools, it does not hallucinate numbers
RAG over pgvector for portfolio Q&A
Embedded MCP server so external agents can query the same engine
One `docker compose up`, no API keys, three seeded demo personas
lessons: Let the model narrate, never calculate. Every number in the prose comes from a tool call you can point at.

name: VolForecast
tagline: MLOps platform forecasting short-horizon volatility, benchmarked honestly vs GARCH.
description: Realized-volatility forecasting for crypto and equities wrapped in a full MLOps lifecycle: leak-free walk-forward evaluation against GARCH/EWMA/HAR baselines, champion/challenger registry in MLflow, QLIKE-gated promotion, drift detection and automated retraining.
architecture: Prefect orchestrates the lifecycle; MLflow holds the champion/challenger registry; LightGBM does the forecasting; FastAPI serves and Streamlit inspects. Promotion is gated on QLIKE against the baselines.
highlights: Leak-free walk-forward evaluation — no peeking, ever
Benchmarked against GARCH, EWMA and HAR instead of a strawman
Champion/challenger registry with QLIKE-gated promotion
Drift detection triggers automated retraining
Covers both crypto and equities
lessons: A vol model that can't beat HAR isn't a model, it's a plot. Building the baselines first made the whole project honest.

name: Solo Strength Quest
tagline: A fitness RPG — every workout is a quest, every PR is a boss kill.
description: Gamified training app: workouts become quests, progressive overload becomes XP, and your profile is a character sheet that levels up because you did. Rust/Axum API with server-side gamification math, Flutter app with a custom design system, Postgres + Redis underneath.
architecture: Rust/Axum API owns all gamification maths server-side — the client never decides what an XP award is. SQLx over Postgres, Redis for hot state, Flutter client with its own design system.
highlights: Workouts become quests; progressive overload becomes XP
Personal records land as boss kills and level-ups
All gamification maths server-side — clients can't mint XP
Flutter client with a hand-built design system
Playable web demo published separately
lessons: Third attempt at this app. The two rewrites before it died of client-side game logic and no schema discipline.

name: One Piece Guess
tagline: Wordle, but for One Piece — a daily character riddle picked by a cron job.
description: Guess the daily character: eight attribute clues per guess (crew, bounty, haki, fruit, debut saga…), hints that unlock as you struggle, a shareable emoji grid. A GitHub Actions cron picks a new pirate every morning; the README doubles as a guide to building your own daily-anything game.
architecture: Entirely static. A GitHub Actions cron runs a Python picker each morning, commits the day's character, and Pages redeploys. No backend to keep alive.
highlights: Eight attribute clues per guess: crew, bounty, haki, devil fruit, debut saga and more
Hints unlock as you struggle; shareable emoji grid at the end
New pirate every morning, chosen by a cron job
README doubles as a how-to for building your own daily-anything game
Embedded and playable on this site's Play tab
lessons: The whole 'daily game' genre is one cron job and a committed JSON file. Everything else is decoration.

name: Side by Side
tagline: A self-updating Collingwood super-fan suite — reskinnable for any AFL club.
description: Next-game countdown, form guide, live ladder and a daily news sweep, rebuilt every morning by a cron job from the free Squiggle API and Google News. Everything club-specific lives in one config file — fork it, edit club.json, and it's your club's suite.
architecture: Same shape as One Piece Guess: cron job, Python fetcher, committed JSON, static Pages. Everything club-specific is isolated in `club.json` so the suite reskins by config, not by fork-and-edit.
highlights: Next-game countdown, form guide and live ladder from the free Squiggle API
Daily news sweep via Google News
Reskins to any AFL club by editing one config file
Rebuilt every morning by a cron job — nothing to host
lessons: Config file over fork. Making the club swappable took an hour and turned a personal page into something anyone can use.

name: Gartic Hands
tagline: Multiplayer draw-and-guess where you draw with webcam hand tracking.
description: Gartic Phone, except players draw with their hands in front of a webcam via MediaPipe hand tracking. Server-held round state machine drives the full party loop. Built with a Monash FIT3170 team.
architecture: MediaPipe hand tracking in the browser turns a webcam into a brush. Round state lives on an Express + Socket.IO server so no client can desync the party loop. Dockerised for the team.
highlights: Draw with your hands in front of a webcam — no mouse, no stylus
Server-held round state machine drives the full Gartic-style loop
Real-time multiplayer over Socket.IO
Built with a Monash FIT3170 team — the only group project in the index
lessons: Hand tracking is the easy half. Keeping eight browsers agreed on whose turn it is was the actual project.

name: smartc
tagline: CLI wizard that writes compile-verified smart contracts plus deploy docs.
description: Single-binary Node CLI: short wizard in, one contract file plus a DEPLOY.md with copy-pasteable commands out. ERC-20/721/1155 and Solana SPL templates, every Solidity contract compiled in-process before it touches disk. Optional local-only AI patching via Ollama.
architecture: One Node binary. Wizard collects intent, templates emit Solidity or Anchor, solc compiles in-process, and only verified output hits disk. Ollama patching is opt-in and local-only.
highlights: ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155 and Solana SPL templates
Every Solidity contract compiled in-process before it's written out
Emits a DEPLOY.md with copy-pasteable commands, not just a contract
Optional AI patching runs locally through Ollama — nothing leaves your machine
Published on npm; MIT licensed
lessons: Refuse to write a file that doesn't compile. It turns a code generator into a tool you can trust half-asleep.

name: Contact Flow
tagline: A production-shaped contact and lead-capture stack, one docker compose up.
description: Contact/lead-capture done the way a real product would do it: NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL API, Next.js 14 + Tailwind frontend, validation implemented properly on both sides rather than trusted from the client. Whole stack comes up with one docker compose command.
architecture: NestJS + TypeORM over Postgres on the API side, Next.js 14 App Router with Tailwind on the front. Validation schemas run in both places; the server never trusts the client's word for it.
highlights: Validation done properly on both sides — the server re-checks everything
NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL API with real layering
Next.js 14 + Tailwind frontend
One `docker compose up` brings the whole stack
lessons: 'Simple CRUD form' is the best place to practise the boring parts — layering, validation, migrations — where nothing exotic hides the mistakes.

name: TODO List
tagline: A deliberately simple todo app built like a real codebase — .NET + Angular.
description: A todo app that is deliberately boring on the surface and deliberately rigorous underneath: .NET Web API with proper layering, Angular frontend with presentational components, tests on both sides. Subtasks, inline edit, active/completed tabs. Built as a reference implementation for how a small app should actually be structured.
architecture: .NET Web API split into real layers — controllers, services, data — rather than one fat controller. Angular front end keeps components presentational and pushes state up. Both halves have tests.
highlights: Subtasks, inline edit, and active/completed tabs
Proper layering in the API instead of logic in controllers
Presentational Angular components with state kept above them
Tests on both the .NET and the Angular side
lessons: The point was never the todo app. It was having one small codebase where the structure is right, to compare bigger ones against.

name: Exaryn Studio
tagline: This site — portfolio, daily AI signal digest, and the Obsidian brain.
description: The studio's own site: a pure static portfolio with no framework and no build step, a self-updating daily AI digest rebuilt every morning by a GitHub Actions cron, and the Exaryn Brain — an Obsidian vault of markdown notes about everything built here, browsable in-page with backlinks and a graph view.
architecture: No framework, no build step. HTML pages fetch JSON out of `/data`; Python scripts in `/scripts` regenerate that JSON on a cron; GitHub Actions commits the result and redeploys Pages.
highlights: Zero dependencies — the whole site is HTML, CSS and one JS file per surface
Daily AI digest with a browsable day-by-day archive
Repo metadata swept from the GitHub API into `data/repos.json`
The Exaryn Brain: a real Obsidian vault, readable in the browser
Everything regenerates on one morning cron
lessons: A static site that regenerates itself is the cheapest infrastructure there is. The cron job is the whole backend.

name: JSON API Simplifier
tagline: Strip a JSON API response down to its shape so you can read the contract.
description: A small Python utility: paste in a real API response, get back the same structure with all the values emptied out. Makes it obvious what fields an endpoint actually returns, so you stop misreading a value for a schema when wiring up calls.
architecture: One script. Walk the parsed JSON, keep keys and container types, drop leaf values.
highlights: Turns a fat API response into a readable shape
Removes the risk of mistaking one sample value for the field's type
Small enough to paste into anything
lessons: The smallest tool in the index and one of the most reused. Structure is the thing you need; the sample data is noise.

name: PDF Compiler
tagline: An early browser-side document compiler — the oldest thing still in the index.
description: An early experiment in assembling and compiling documents in the browser. Kept in the index as the honest starting point: it predates the studio, has no tests, and is here because the timeline should include the beginning, not just the parts that went well.
architecture: Browser-side only. No build, no server, no tests.
highlights: The oldest surviving project in the index
Kept unchanged as a before-picture
lessons: Left as-is on purpose. Every index should contain at least one thing you'd write differently now.
